Are businesses doing enough to protect your data? | CBC News Loaded Business Data breaches are coming fast and furious. Are businesses doing enough to protect your data? Recent data breaches at Bell and Staples are the latest in a swath of incidents where consumers' personal data was accessed by bad actors. As AI tools make it easier to carry out hacks, many businesses are trying to keep up with the onslaught of attacks — but security and data experts say poor data management and security practices often leave consumer information more vulnerable than it should be. As AI makes cyber incidents more likely, experts say some businesses are taking the threat seriously, but many are still leaving their customers' personal data exposed. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters) Social Sharing First it was a data breach at Staples , with the company alerting staplesprint.ca customers Friday that some personal information was accessed in a recent security incident. Then came a notice from Bell , saying an "agentic threat actor" had accessed personal information like names, phone numbers and email addresses, impacting customers of Bell, Bell Aliant, Bell MTS, Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile. Agentic usually refers to AI tools that can act independently. The incidents are just the latest examples of breaches — Loblaws , Save-on-Foods , Montreal car-sharing company Communauto and telecomm provider Eastlink have all made headlines for data incidents in the past few months. For Bell customers like Anna Stephenson, who received an email this week saying her data might have been compromised, news of another hack doesn't feel all that surprising anymore. "It's kind of the world we live in now where we have to sort of deal with these things," she said. Bell says cybersecurity incident affected customers at Virgin Plus, Lucky Mobile AI-powered Bell hack a sign of things to come, cybersecurity firm says Though she understands Bell's challenge in staying one step ahead of criminals, Stephenson wants to see companies do more to protect the valuable data they keep about customers. "In my opinion, companies need to invest more in that security, and hopefully that's something that Bell's looking into," Stephenson said. The experts agree. As AI tools make it easier to carry out hacks, lots of businesses are trying to keep up with the onslaught of attacks — but security and data experts say poor data management and security practices often leave consumer information more vulnerable than it should be. Too much data, not enough protection Canadian privacy laws require companies to follow 10 principles when collecting, using and safeguarding personal information.
